paragraphs.text: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Its features include an unusual facial appearance, cleft lip/palate, ectodermal dysplasia with hypotrichosis and dental anomalies, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and onychodysplasia, and cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers and/or toes. Some patients have mental retardation (Suzuki et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2015). Sözen et al. (2001) found that heterozygosity for a PVRL1 nonsense mutation was associated with sporadic, nonsyndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate (OFC7) in northern Venezuela.

paragraphs.text: Bustos et al. (1991) described 27 individuals from 7 families on Margarita Island in northeastern Venezuela (Nueva Esparta State). The families were very probably related to one another and came from a relatively isolated, inbred population. Patients had ectodermal dysplasia and other anomalies, and expressivity was variable. Females were affected as severely as males, and all parents were normal. The authors could not classify the condition among the known ectodermal dysplasias and considered it a newly recognized autosomal recessive dysplasia/malformation syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Yoshida et al. (2015) reported a 7-year-old Japanese boy who was the first child of a consanguineous marriage. He had hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with sparse, brittle, fine, dry hair and hypodontia, along with the characteristic facial appearance with cleft lip/palate, cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers, and mild mental retardation. Scanning electron microscopy of the hair showed pili torti and pili trianguli et canaliculi.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora et al. (1987) considered autosomal recessive inheritance most likely, based on 2 affected sibs. Affected sibs born to consanguineous parents were reported by Oğur and Yüksel (1988) and by Rodini and Richieri-Costa (1990). In the Margarita Island families, Bustos et al. (1991) found that females were affected as severely as males and that all parents were normal, which supports autosomal recessive inheritance. Yoshida et al. (2015) found that the parents of a patient with a homozygous PVRL1 mutation were both heterozygous carriers.
